figures.caption: Isolated Spread Footing
figures.description: Isolated Spread Footings Single column support where loads can be distributed to adequate bearing material through an individual footing. Designed to distribute concentrated column loads and prevent shear failure of bearing material Typical minimum size for bridge columns is 3 m x 3 m (10 ft x 10 ft) Footing size increases with eccentric loads Sizing depends on column loads and bearing material strength/compressibility Structural design considers moment resistance at column face, shear, and punching shear

figures.caption: Continuous Strip Spread Footing
figures.description: Continuous Strip Spread Footings Support of bearing walls or a single row of columns where continuous load distribution is needed. Most common foundation type for buildings Minimum length-to-width ratio of at least 5 (length > 5 x width) Supports a single row of columns or a bearing wall Plane strain conditions assumed parallel to the long axis Structural design governed by beam shear and bending moments Can tie columns together in one direction

figures.caption: Spread Footing with Cantilever Stemwall at Bridge Abutment
figures.description: Bridge Abutments Bridge abutment design where the foundation must serve both structural support and earth retention functions. Abutments must retain backfill, support superstructure, provide approach fill transition, and accommodate thermal movements Spread footings with cantilever stemwalls are well suited for these multiple functions Must distribute superstructure loads to bearing materials below the footing

figures.caption: Semi-Gravity Cantilever Retaining Wall
figures.description: Retaining Structures Semi-gravity concrete cantilever retaining wall design where the base footing provides foundation support and overturning resistance. Semi-gravity cantilever retaining walls (inverted T-walls) use shallow spread footings as their base The wall resists loads by the dead weight of backfill on the heel and the structural cantilever of the stem

figures.caption: Combined Footing
figures.description: Combination Footings Multiple-column support where individual footings would overlap or where non-uniform column spacing or large overturning moments are present. Support two or more columns on a single rectangular or trapezoidal footing Used when column spacing is non-uniform (Bowles, 1996) or isolated footings become so closely spaced that a combined footing is simpler to form and build Spill-through abutments are a bridge application of combination footings (Figure 2-6) Frame action allows resistance to large overturning or rotational moments Spill-through abutments used at stream crossings to place foundations below scour level Design choice depends on available space, load distribution, soil variability, and economics

figures.caption: Spill-Through Abutment on Combination Strip Footing
figures.description: Combination Footings Multiple-column support where individual footings would overlap or where non-uniform column spacing or large overturning moments are present. Support two or more columns on a single rectangular or trapezoidal footing Used when column spacing is non-uniform (Bowles, 1996) or isolated footings become so closely spaced that a combined footing is simpler to form and build Spill-through abutments are a bridge application of combination footings (Figure 2-6) Frame action allows resistance to large overturning or rotational moments Spill-through abutments used at stream crossings to place foundations below scour level Design choice depends on available space, load distribution, soil variability, and economics

figures.caption: Typical Mat Foundation
figures.description: Mat Foundations Structures where spread footings would cover more than 50% of the plan area, or where differential settlement must be minimized over weak or variable ground conditions. Single heavily reinforced concrete slab underlying the entire structure or major portion Economical when spread footings would cover more than about 50% of the plan area (Peck et al. 1974) Principal advantage is ability to bridge over soft spots and reduce differential movement Suitable for relatively weak soils or lightweight structures Limited applicability for bridge support; applicable for bascule piers and movable bridge supports Common transportation applications include maintenance facilities, storage bins, and box culverts Large mat foundation design discussed in Section 8.6

figures.caption: Typical Shallow Foundations on IGM or Rock for Highway and Bridge Structures
figures.description: Footings on Intermediate Geomaterials (IGMs) and Rock Shallow foundation design on intermediate geomaterials and rock, including assessment of discontinuities, slope stability, and potential for strength loss or cavern collapse. IGMs are materials too dense/stiff for 'soil' classification but not intact 'rock' (glacial till, weathered rock, indurated sediments, cemented materials) IGMs are strong and stiff enough that considerations other than strength (e.g., overturning potential) typically govern Three foundation configurations on IGM/rock: horizontal bearing, near-slope crest, and tied-in for uplift/lateral loads (Figure 3-1) Slope stability analysis for IGM/rock must consider planar, wedge, sliding, and toppling failure mechanisms Evaluate weathering degree, rock strength, durability,

figures.caption: Correlation Between Relative Density and SPT Resistance (NAVFAC, 1986a, after Gibbs & Holtz)
figures.description: Standard Penetration Test SPT testing procedures, N-value correlations, and hammer efficiency corrections for foundation design. SPT standardized by AASHTO T-206 and ASTM D-1586 63-kg hammer, 0.76 m drop; N-value = sum of blows for second and third 150-mm increments N-values correlate with relative density (sands) and consistency (clays) per Table 4-1 Figures 4-1 and 4-2 relate N-value to relative density and friction angle for granular soils Figure 4-1 is a function of both N-value and effective overburden stress; do not correct N for overburden Hammer efficiency correction: N60 = (ER/60%) * N_field (Equation 4-1) Automatic hammers typically have 70-90% efficiency; 80% commonly assumed Correlations for gravels and clays from SPT are relatively unreliable

figures.caption: Phase Relation Block Diagram
figures.description: Phase and Volume Relationships Fundamental soil phase relationships and weight-volume computations for geotechnical design. Soil is a three-phase material: solid, water, gas (air) Phase relationships defined by specific gravity, void space, and degree of saturation Void ratio (e) is a general indicator of relative strength and compressibility Low void ratio indicates strong, incompressible soils; high void ratio indicates weak, compressible soils Table 4-3 contains Equations 4-2 through 4-20 for all weight-volume and functional relationships Consolidation occurs as excess pore-water pressure dissipates and intergranular stress increases Spring analogy (Figure 4-4) explains consolidation: valve = permeability, spring = soil skeleton, water = pore fluid

figures.caption: Conceptual Arrangement of Laboratory Oedometer Test
figures.description: Principle of Effective Stress Fundamental principle governing soil strength, compressibility, and consolidation behavior. Total stress = pore-water pressure + effective stress (Equation 4-21: sigma' = sigma - u) Pore-water pressure acts equally in all directions and has no shear strength Only effective (intergranular) stress resists shearing and controls compression Changes in effective stress control volumetric strain development In saturated clay loaded quickly, pore pressure initially carries the entire applied load Over time, excess pore pressure dissipates and effective stress increases (consolidation) Oedometer test (Figure 4-5) demonstrates this principle in the laboratory

figures.caption: Allowable Bearing Capacity Controlled by Shear Failure Considerations versus Settlement Considerations
figures.description: Allowable Bearing Capacity Conceptual framework for all shallow foundation bearing capacity evaluation. Allowable bearing capacity combines shear failure prevention and settlement limitation Both are functions of the least footing dimension, the footing width B (or B_f) For a surface footing on isotropic, homogeneous material, FS against shear failure increases with B As B increases the depth of influence also increases: the stress increase reaches deeper below the bearing elevation Narrow footings: shear failure controls the allowable bearing capacity; wide footings: settlement controls (Figure 5-1)

figures.caption: Bearing Capacity Failure of Silo Foundation (Vesic, 1975, from Tschebotarioff, 1951)
figures.description: Bearing Capacity Theory All shallow foundations where shear failure must be evaluated. Ultimate bearing capacity is the load that causes subsurface collapse due to insufficient soil strength Foundation failure manifests as excessive penetration or rotation Settlement involves both immediate elastic strains and long-term consolidation Bearing capacity theory provides the framework for preventing shear failure

figures.caption: Boundaries of Zone of Plastic Equilibrium after Failure of Soil Beneath Continuous Footing
figures.description: General Shear Recognizing the general shear failure mode that bearing capacity theory describes. Prandtl (1920) and Reissner (1924) derived the strain states of a weightless rigid-plastic soil at ultimate bearing capacity Zones (Terzaghi & Peck, 1948): I elastic wedge moving down with the footing; II radial shear on a logarithmic spiral; III passive state at 45 - phi'/2 from horizontal General shear: well-defined shear planes to the surface, footing rotation, bulging on both sides Prevailing mode for relatively incompressible, reasonably strong soils and for saturated NC clays loaded rapidly (undrained) (Coduto, 1994)

figures.description: Bearing Capacity Equation Formulations All bearing capacity calculations for shallow foundations. Use Eq 5-7 as the base equation before applying correction factors. figures.description: Sloping Ground Surface Footings located on slopes or within 2-6 footing widths of a slope crest. figures.description: Global Stability All shallow foundations near slopes or on ground with non-level geometry. figures.caption: Coulomb Lateral Earth Pressure Definitions

figures.description: Effective Footing Dimensions and Overturning Stability Computing effective footing dimensions for eccentric loading and checking overturning stability.
